title: May I be a medicine
hook: honey on a spoon, ginger in a mug; Shantideva wishes to be the medicine itself
tomorrow: medicine was one. what else does he wish to be?

segments.voice: Yesterday: rejoicing. Being glad for other people's good on purpose, even the one who beat you. Glad for all. Today the gladness turns into a wish, and it has a taste.
screen: `GLAD FOR ALL.` → `NOW A WISH, WITH A TASTE.`

segments.voice: A spoonful of honey for a sore throat. A mug of ginger tea, too hot to drink, with steam that clears your nose before the first sip. The bitter little pill somebody cut in half for you when you were small. Medicine has a taste, and it usually comes with a person: whoever stood at the stove, or held out the spoon. So, yesterday's riddle: what does Shantideva wish he were, that you'd swallow? He wishes to be the medicine.
screen: `HONEY ON A SPOON.` → `GINGER, TOO HOT TO DRINK.` → `HE WISHES TO BE THE MEDICINE.`

segments.voice: Chapter three, right after rejoicing. Shantideva makes a run of wishes, and here is one of them. For everyone in the world who is sick, may I be the medicine, the doctor and the nurse, until the sickness never comes back. Notice there are three roles, and he wants all of them. The doctor knows what's wrong. The nurse stays through the night. And the medicine is the strangest wish of all. It gets used up. It disappears into the person who needs it, and nobody thanks the pill. The very next verse pushes further: in a famine, may I fall like rain as food and drink. This is an aspiration, a wish said with the whole heart, the kind the awakening mind runs on. It doesn't claim he can cure anyone yet. It points his whole life toward being of use. And it reaches the ordinary scale, too. Nobody has to be a doctor to be someone's medicine: the cup of tea, the honey on the spoon, the person who sits with you while the pill works. May I be the medicine.
screen: `MEDICINE, DOCTOR AND NURSE.` · `MEDICINE GETS USED UP.` · `RAIN AS FOOD IN A FAMINE.` · `A WISH THAT POINTS A LIFE.` · then, large: `MAY I BE THE MEDICINE.`

segments.voice: If you have a warm drink or even a glass of water, hold it in both hands and take one slow sip, noticing the warmth or the cool on your tongue. Then bring one person to mind who isn't feeling well, in body or in heart. Let the next sips be for them, and see one small way you could help them feel better.
May I be a medicine: Shantideva's wish to be medicine, doctor and nurse for all who are sick, until no one is.
screen: `MAY I BE A MEDICINE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: may I be the medicine. Most medicine comes in a cup and a kind hand. Twelve days into the poem.

howItsDone: Mahayana Buddhists recite verses from this part of chapter three as aspirations, and the Medicine Buddha, Bhaisajyaguru, is honored in East Asian and Tibetan Buddhism as a Buddha of healing.

myth: Shantideva claims he can already cure every illness
it's an aspiration: a wish that points his life toward being of use, not a claim of power.
he wishes to be the medicine, the doctor and the nurse
all three roles, until the sickness never comes back.
being someone's medicine requires medical training
the wish reaches ordinary life: a cup of tea, a spoon of honey, someone who stays.

fork.setup: your roommate has the flu and you have a big deadline. what fits Shantideva's wish?
options: stay away completely; you can't be useful if you get sick too.
drop the deadline and stay by her bed all day.
leave tea and soup at her door, check in by text, and keep working.
fork.reveal: the wish is to be medicine where you are. a cup by the door and a message are small, real ways of being someone's medicine.

original.note: Sanskrit: medicine, remedy. The same word is in the name of the Medicine Buddha, Bhaisajyaguru.

trapdoor: what you thought: the verse is a nice way of saying be helpful.
what it means: Shantideva wishes to be medicine, doctor and nurse for all who are sick, and even to fall as food in a famine.
what a scholar hears: an aspiration (pranidhana) in the chapter on taking up the awakening mind, one of a run of wishes that later Mahayana practice recites as its own.

chat.meaning: Shantideva wishes to be medicine, doctor and nurse. Ordinary care, someone who stays and does it with you, is part of that wish.
